open-question.alternative: The extension is published to no registry and no release page while it is an experiment: it is packaged as a VSIX and installed by hand into the maintainer's own editor (built from source by anyone else who wants it), and the draft records registry publication as deferred, not ruled out, to be decided once the experiment is judged. The one venue the draft's 2026-11-17 check covered, read by default by the VS Code the maintainer works in, with search, update notices, and automatic updates, at one publisher account and one publish step per release. Forks that read another registry by default (VSCodium and the other editors built on VS Code that use Open VSX) do not reach it, and the Marketplace's terms limit its use to Microsoft's products; it also creates the permanent publisher id and reserves the extension name for good while the extension is still an experiment, binding whatever name the sibling naming question settles.

The extension is published to the Visual Studio Marketplace and to the Open VSX registry the forks read, both from the first release and with the same version each time. Every editor built on VS Code installs and updates it from its own default registry, so a collaborator or user on a fork is reached as the maintainer on VS Code is. Two publisher accounts, two tokens, two namespaces whose ids and names are reserved, and two publish steps on every release of a fourth artifact beside the three host trees, for a plugin with few users; publication outside the Marketplace is unchecked in the draft, so this rests on a venue whose rules nobody has read, which depends on whether the sibling question on further VS Code checks has it checked.

open-question.question: When a task runs under a host, model, and effort chosen for it, is its command line one of the recipe file's own single-task lines picked by name, so the extension still holds no host flag, model name, or effort level of its own, or does the extension compose the line from the three values and so hold each host's command syntax?
open-question.recommendation: Each profile stays a complete line a person can paste, as the snippet file's two single-task lines already are, so the extension still holds no host flag, model name, or effort level and a task's assignment only names a line. The combinations in real use are few (a default, a stronger model for generation work, another host), so the number of lines to keep stays small.
open-question.alternative: The recipe file holds complete single-task lines, one per host, model, and effort combination wanted, each under a name of its own and each in the form the snippet file already has (`claude -p "/gurita:complete-task --mission <path> <Task Title>" ... --model "opus" --effort xhigh`, `agy -p ... --model "claude-opus-5-5" --effort high`). A task's chosen combination is a reference to one of those names; the extension picks the named line and fills only `<path>` and `<Task Title>`. It holds no host flag, model name, or effort level, and "The constraint" and the Recipes part stand as written. Keeps the draft's constraint exactly as it stands, with every host's syntax only as text in lines a person can paste and run by hand, the way the snippet file's two single-task lines already run today, so nothing new enters the extension and no host change can break code of its own. Every combination used is a line to write and keep, so lines multiply with hosts times models times efforts and a combination nobody wrote cannot be chosen; the choice of a task's run becomes a choice of a line name, which holds only if the way per-task assignments are kept (the per-task assignment question's axis) can name a line rather than three values.

The recipe file holds one single-task line per host with two new placeholders beside `<path>` and `<Task Title>`, such as `<model>` and `<effort>`, in the positions that host's flags take (`--model "<model>" --effort <effort>` on Claude Code and Antigravity; on Codex `-m "<model>"` and no effort position, since it has no effort flag). The chosen host picks the template, and the extension substitutes the chosen model and effort as plain values the way it fills any placeholder; the host's command syntax stays text in the recipe, while the model and effort values come from wherever the task's choice is kept rather than from the extension's code. The notation gains the two placeholders. Any model and effort a host accepts can be chosen with one line per host, so the line count stays at the number of hosts while the extension still holds no host flag syntax and every template remains a pasteable line. Adds two placeholders to the recipe notation and a rule for a template that lacks a position (Codex's effort, silently ignored), and a value the host refuses (an `xhigh` on `agy`, a model id written in another host's form) surfaces only as that run's stop, since nothing checks the value against the host before the run; how far the draft's "no model name or effort level" wording must be reworded depends on where the per-task assignment question keeps the values.

The extension builds each single-task line from the three values itself: it holds, per host, the binary and headless form (`claude -p`, `agy -p`, `codex exec`), the prompt's sigil and quoting (`"/gurita:..."` against `'$gurita:...'`), the permission flag, and the model and effort flags (`--model`/`--effort`, Codex's `-m` with no effort), the rules the legend of `docs/ways-of-using.md` states for moving a line between hosts. The recipe file holds no single-task line, and "The constraint" and the Recipes part are rewritten to say the extension holds each host's command syntax for this one line. Any host, model, and effort combination runs with no line written by anyone, and the extension can check a combination before the run (Antigravity's `high` ceiling, Codex's missing effort flag) and offer only the values each host takes. Puts a second copy of each host's command syntax in the extension's code beside the legend, which drifts when a host renames a flag or a model id form, and breaks the draft's constraint that all host-specific text lives in lines a person could type, so the composed line is no longer one a recipe file shows or a person can edit.

A stdlib-only tool added to the plugin's tools takes a host, model, effort, mission path, and task title and prints the complete headless `complete-task` line for that host; the extension runs it from the plugin's installed copy and executes what it prints, holding no host syntax itself, while the per-host rules move from the legend's prose into that tested tool, which the legend may then describe. The draft's "no plugin change" consequence is rewritten. Gives the host syntax one tested home shipped with the plugin that knows its own hosts, so the extension and any other runner, Kepala included, compose the same line without holding a copy of their own. Turns a draft for an extension into a plugin change, a fifth tool kind (one that prints commands for other hosts) the plugin has never had, and needs the plugin's installed location found per host, which stays open under the live-state question; the line it prints is still invisible to a person until it runs.

The revision does not settle the line's source now: it lists, among the draft's questions for the work, whether a per-task line is a named recipe line, a per-host template, or composed, with those options written out, and the Recipes part and "The constraint" stay as written until the work answers it. Keeps the revision from fixing a mechanism before per-task running and its assignment have been tried, at the cost of nothing the draft says today. Leaves an adopted per-task loop with no stated way to build its lines, so the draft describes a feature whose one host-facing step is open and whose fit with its own constraint is unknown; it holds only if the task-loop question adopts the loop in some form, and is moot otherwise.

open-question.question: What is the extension named: a name that joins Gurita and Kepala, or a descriptive one? Whichever it is, its slug is to get the direct registry lookup `ideas/gurita.md` records its own first check lacked.
open-question.alternative: Name family: descriptive, carrying the plugin's name with a qualifier. The display name is a description such as Gurita for VS Code or Gurita Missions, and the slug its lowercase form, such as `gurita-vscode`. Lookup: this mission looks the exact slug up directly on the extension registries and on GitHub, and records the dated result in the draft; the `gurita` stem is already covered by the 2026-11-10 lookup. It says what the extension is and what it serves without a sentence, is found by a search for Gurita, coins no word, needs only one narrow lookup, and leaves both Kepala and Kepalagurita untouched whatever the Kepala boundary question settles. It steps outside the head-and-arms image, so if the extension later grows into the orchestrator's interface its name does not carry over and a published name cannot be taken back. A `vscode` qualifier also reads oddly on a VS Code fork, and which registries the lookup must cover depends on the Publication venue question.

Name family: the head word already on record. The extension is named Kepala, display name and slug `kepala`, the name `ideas/kepala.md` gives the orchestrator. Lookup: this mission looks `kepala` up directly on the registries the extension could be published to and on GitHub, and records the dated result in the draft, which also discharges the lookup `ideas/kepala.md` requires before anything is published under that name. It coins nothing: the name, its meaning, and its image are already written down, and the draft's Kepala section already calls the extension's runner Kepala's transition engine with a person choosing the edge, so the extension becomes the head over the arms with no further naming work. It spends the orchestrator's name on an experiment the 2026-11-19 conversation says a deeper integration or an application of its own may follow, and an extension name once published and removed is reserved for good. It holds only where the extension is a first form of Kepala, which the Kepala boundary question decides, and if Kepala's repeated lookup fails, the extension and the orchestrator lose their name together.

Name family: the compound on record. The extension is named Kepalagurita, display name and slug `kepalagurita`, the one-word name `ideas/kepala.md` gives the whole. Lookup: this mission looks `kepalagurita` up directly on the extension's registries and on GitHub, and records the dated result in the draft. It names the extension as an interface over the whole, the head and the arms together, which fits a pane that drives every phase of a mission by buttons, and it leaves Kepala free for the orchestrator. `ideas/kepala.md` reserves Kepalagurita as an organisation or umbrella name and leaves open where it lands, so giving it to one product takes that question over. It is twelve letters, which that draft accepted only because the name would be typed rarely, and a name this broad suits an experiment poorly if a deeper integration later replaces it.

Name family: a new name in the same image. This mission chooses a third Indonesian word for a part of the octopus that joins Gurita as Kepala does, for example Mata, the eye, for the reading and watching interface, with its merged form (Matagurita) beside it. The draft records why the word fits, lists the words it ruled out with a one-line reason each, as the naming drafts do, and records a dated direct lookup of each slug on the registries and on GitHub. The extension gets a name of its own that states its role in the image, distinct from the orchestrator, so whatever the Kepala boundary question settles, neither name has to change for the other. It is a naming exercise of the size of the two naming drafts inside a mission whose subject is the extension's design: a third foreign word to explain on the landing page, no candidate on record, and short common words such as `mata` likely to be crowded on the registries, so the choice may take several rounds of lookups.

Name family: the plugin's own name, unqualified. The extension's display name is Gurita and its slug `gurita`, the extension standing as the plugin's VS Code face. Lookup: this mission looks `gurita` up directly on the extension registries, which the 2026-11-10 lookup did not cover (it covered npm, PyPI, crates.io, and GitHub), and records the dated result in the draft. Anyone who knows the plugin finds the extension under the one name they already search for, and nothing new has to be coined or explained. It names two products one thing, against the reason `ideas/gurita.md` and `ideas/kepala.md` give for a second name, that a product sitting on top of the plugin needs a name saying how it relates to it: a person installing the extension could take it for the plugin, which it does not install, and the two would be released separately under one name.

Name family and lookup: neither now. The revised draft keeps "the extension has no name of its own yet" and lists the name among the questions left for the work, with the slug's direct registry lookup due before anything is published, as `ideas/kepala.md` sets its own lookup. The name is chosen once the extension's shape, its relation to Kepala, its repository, and its publication venue are settled and its first version is about to be published, the one point at which a permanent publisher id and extension name start to matter. The goal asks the mission to settle the draft's ten questions, and this one is settled only by moving it on: the draft carries the same open question into the work, and a lookup made later may find the preferred slug taken by then.
